summary:
We built Phnx, a web app that turns 26 years of NASA FIRMS satellite fire detections (about 363 million hotspots) into one consistent burning activity calendar.

MODIS holds the long record but is near the end of its mission. VIIRS sees far more small fires, and each new VIIRS satellite adds overpasses. If you simply add the raw detections up, fire activity jumps in 2018 and doubles in 2023 without any extra fire. Phnx fixes this by calibrating everything to today's VIIRS constellation. 

Users pick any area and any period. They can then see when and where it burned, monthly anomalies against the median, trends, a seasonal forecast, and individual detections on a WebGL map.

This matters because emergency managers, scientists and land managers need a fire record where long-term trends reflect real fire, not changing satellites. That will be even more important once MODIS is retired and the data is potentially lost.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

We set out to answer a simple question: when and where has it burned, and is it getting worse? To do that, we combined 26 years of NASA FIRMS fire detections into one consistent burning activity calendar. That's about 363 million hotspots from the MODIS and VIIRS sensors.

You pick an area by drawing it on the map or typing a country, region or city. Then you pick a period. Phnx shows how much burned in each month, week or day and how that compares with the same month in other years. It also shows the overall trend and a forecast for the rest of the year. On the map you can zoom in to individual detections, watch fires move over time, and lay real daily satellite images underneath.

The core problem is that the two sensors don't see fire the same way. VIIRS picks up far more small fires than MODIS, and each new VIIRS satellite adds more overpasses. In the raw data, fire activity seems to jump in 2018 and double in 2023, even though there was no real change on the ground. So we calibrated everything to today's VIIRS satellites. Older MODIS data is converted separately for each grid cell and each calendar month, because the gap between the sensors depends on the place and the season. When we tested it, the converted MODIS series matched VIIRS within about 2%, and the old jumps disappeared.


WHY IT MATTERS

MODIS is nearing the end of its mission, and without harmonization, a change of satellite can easily be mistaken for a real change on the ground. We want fire managers, researchers and land managers to have a fire record they can trust, where 2005 and today can be compared directly.


HOW WE BUILT IT

We had very little time, so we kept the setup lean. The backend is Python with FastAPI and DuckDB working directly on Parquet files. That let us process the whole dataset on a small server with 4 cores and 8 GB RAM. Statsmodels handles the forecasts. The frontend is one web page built with MapLibre GL, deck.gl and Plotly. We used Claude as a coding and writing assistant to move fast. The method and the product decisions were ours, and we checked the results ourselves.


WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Instead of one global correction factor, our calibration adapts to the place and the season. The map also switches automatically between single points, smooth heatmaps and aggregated grids. That way, hundreds of millions of detections can still run in an ordinary browser.


WHAT WE KEPT IN MIND

Even under time pressure, we didn't want to cut corners on honesty. Converted months are visibly marked, forecasts are clearly labelled, and the original detections stay available. We want Phnx to be open to everyone: no accounts, colour palettes that are safe for colour-blind users, and data that anyone can download and check.
